args.text: [lane-vole] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server after a site moves or fails over, so they see errors or outdated content. (2) Slow recovery: if a bad or poisoned answer is cached, it stays in place until the cache expires, prolonging the harm. (3) Delayed changes: updates such as security fixes, traffic shifts or certificate-related moves take longer to reach everyone, and timing is unknown in advance.

args.text: [lane-vole] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a client often cannot tell whether a request worked, and it must be able to send it again safely. An idempotent action gives the same result however many times it runs, which prevents duplicate payments, repeated orders or other double effects.

args.text: [lane-vole] UUIDv7 (a Universally Unique Identifier, version 7, which starts with a timestamp) as a primary key has two trade-offs. (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a plain integer, so tables and indexes grow larger and lookups can be slower. (2) Leaked timing: because the creation time is built into the value, anyone who sees an ID can estimate when the record was made. Its order is also only roughly sequential across several machines.

args.text: [lane-vole] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it alters the main data, so the record survives a crash or power cut. After a restart, the database replays the log to finish or undo half-done changes, which keeps the data consistent and avoids losing confirmed work.

args.text: [lane-vole] (1) Fair comparison: a newer client version may change speed, retries or defaults, so unpinned runs could differ because of the client rather than the thing being tested. (2) Repeatability: pinning lets anyone rerun the benchmark later and get comparable results, and it makes any change in numbers easier to trace to a real cause.

args.text: [lane-vole] Backpressure is a way for a busy queue to push back on whoever is adding work, by slowing them down, making them wait or turning requests away, when it cannot keep up. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make every delay worse.

args.text: [lane-vole] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two servers, so both fire at the same moment; (2) a run takes longer than the gap between runs, so the next one starts while the first is still going. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or a database row, and exit quietly if another copy already holds it.

args.text: [lane-vole] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, saying "this was deleted" rather than simply removing it. Without it, a copy that missed the delete could send the old value back to the others, and the deleted item would reappear. Tombstones are cleared away after a set time, once every copy has seen them.

args.text: [lane-vole] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) It passes and fails on the same code, with no change in between, so re-running it gives a different result. (2) The failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or a busy machine, so they appear at random and are hard to repeat on demand.

args.text: [lane-vole] A lease-based lock is a lock that expires after a set time unless renewed. It relies on each machine's clock agreeing on when that time is up. If one clock runs fast or slow, the old holder may think it still has the lock while the lock service thinks it has expired and hands it to someone else. Two machines then act as owner at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. Safer designs add a counter, called a fencing token, that the protected resource checks.
